what: Late interaction (ColBERT) stores one small vector per token instead of one vector per document, then scores a match with MaxSim: every query token looks for its best partner token in the document.
like: Like checking a shopping list item by item against a shelf, instead of comparing a blurry photo of the whole list with a photo of the shelf.
why: Keeps specifics that a single averaged vector washes out, so 'X AND Y' queries match better
Much cheaper than a cross-encoder, because documents are encoded once, offline
Shows which query token matched which document token, so scores are explainable

nodes.t: First stage|BM25 or one dense vector
Top-k|to the LLM or the user

steps.d: A BERT-style encoder turns each token into its own 128-number vector. Documents are encoded once, offline, so a whole passage becomes a small matrix, not one point.
Many vectors per doc means a big index. ColBERTv2 stores each vector as its nearest centroid id plus a 1-2 bit residual; Vespa can binarize a vector to 16 bytes.
BM25, a single dense vector, or PLAID's centroid search quickly picks a few hundred candidates. Late interaction then only has to score those.
For each query token, take the highest dot product with any document token, then add those maxima up. Every query term has to find its own match.
The best passages go to the LLM, which reads and cites them. Per-token matches tell you why each one ranked high.

choices.d: Most teams rerank a few hundred candidates from BM25 or a dense retriever. Full first-stage needs an engine built for it, like PLAID or MUVERA-style single-vector encodings.
Deeper k lifts recall@K but costs more MaxSim work. Measure nDCG@10 and recall at several depths and stop where gains flatten.
Full floats, int8, 2-bit or 1-bit residuals, or binarized vectors. Smaller means cheaper RAM; check nDCG on your own eval set after each step.
ColBERT-style models for text. ColPali embeds page images directly, so tables, charts and layout count without an OCR pipeline.
Vespa (ColBERT embedder, MaxSim in ranking), Qdrant multivectors with MAX_SIM, or Elasticsearch rank_vectors in a script_score rescore.

instead.why: Cross-encoder reads query and doc together: sharper, but slower per candidate
One vector per doc: tiny index and fast, but meaning gets averaged
Exact terms, IDs and names, cheap and strong as a first stage
Blend BM25 and dense lists, then add late interaction on top

breaks.d: One vector per token multiplies storage by document length.
breaks.see: RAM or disk per shard far above your single-vector index
breaks.fix: Residual compression or binarization, token pruning, or keep it rerank-only

breaks.d: Scoring the whole corpus token by token is slow.
breaks.see: p99 latency (slowest 1 in 100) climbs with corpus size
breaks.fix: Cheap first stage, then MaxSim on a few hundred candidates

breaks.d: A reranker cannot rescue a document it never sees.
breaks.see: recall@500 of the first stage is low on the eval set
breaks.fix: Hybrid BM25 + dense first stage, or a deeper candidate list

breaks.d: Too few bits blur fine distinctions.
breaks.see: nDCG@10 or MRR drops after re-indexing
breaks.fix: Step bits back up and A/B on a fixed eval set before rollout

say: A single dense vector averages the whole passage, so a query like 'cheap AND vegan' can match a doc that is only strongly about one of them.
ColBERT keeps one vector per token and scores with MaxSim: each query token takes its best match in the doc, and we sum those.
Because that index is large, I'd retrieve a few hundred candidates with BM25 plus dense, then rescore them with late interaction.
I'd judge it on a labelled set with recall@K for the first stage and nDCG@10 and MRR after rescoring.

followups.q: Why not just use a cross-encoder?
followups.a: A cross-encoder runs the model on every query-doc pair at query time, so cost grows with candidates. Late interaction pre-computes doc vectors offline and only does cheap dot products at query time - often used before a cross-encoder.

followups.q: How do you keep the index size down?
followups.a: ColBERTv2 stores a centroid id plus a 1-2 bit residual per token, about 6-10x smaller. Vespa can binarize to 16 bytes per token. PLAID uses those centroids to prune candidates before full scoring.
Yes with PLAID-style centroid search, or MUVERA, which squeezes the token set into one fixed-length vector for a normal ANN search, then rescores exact MaxSim on the candidates.
A vision-language model that turns a page image into ColBERT-style patch vectors of 128 numbers. Text queries match pages with MaxSim, so tables and charts are searchable without OCR.

today: Late interaction is now a stock feature: Elasticsearch has a rank_vectors field scored with maxSimDotProduct, Qdrant offers MAX_SIM multivectors, and Vespa ships a ColBERT embedder.

check.q: How does MaxSim score a document?
check.a: Best doc-token match for each query token, summed
d: Cosine of the two averaged vectors
check.why: Each query token finds its own best partner, and those best scores add up.

check.q: What is the biggest cost of storing one vector per token?
d: Slower document encoding at query time
check.why: Storage grows with document length. ColBERTv2 compression shrinks it about 6-10x.

check.q: Where is late interaction most often used in a pipeline?
check.a: Rescoring a few hundred first-stage candidates
check.why: A cheap first stage finds candidates, then MaxSim reorders them more precisely.

check.q: Why can one dense vector miss 'cheap AND vegan'?
check.a: It averages the passage into one point
check.why: Averaging blends topics, so one strong topic can outweigh a missing second one.
